title: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): The Gold Standard in Corneal Transplantation
summary: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) remains the definitive full-thickness replacement of diseased corneal tissue with healthy donor graft. This infographic provides a comprehensive clinical framework for surgical management, graft survival, and post-operative care.

sections.title: Definition & Indications
sections.content: PKP involves the full-thickness excision of a central corneal button (donor) and suturing it into the patient's recipient bed. Indications include: Keratoconus (non-progressive), Fuchs Dystrophy, Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK), Corneal Scars (post-trauma/infection), and Chemical Burns.

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Trephination (usually 0.25-0.5mm larger donor than recipient).
Step 2: Removal of diseased recipient cornea with corneal scissors.
Step 3: Positioning donor graft and fixation with four cardinal sutures.
Step 4: Continuous (nylon 10-0) or interrupted suture closure.
Step 5: Assessment of intraoperative keratometry and chamber reformation.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis for Post-Op Red Eye

content.explanation: Khodadoust Line: Endothelial Rejection characterized by an advancing line of white precipitates moving across the donor endothelium toward the graft-host junction.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Advances
content: Topical steroids are the cornerstone of anti-rejection therapy; frequency must be tapered cautiously over 6-12 months.
Always evaluate for 'Glaucoma' in graft failure cases; IOP monitoring is challenging but critical.
Corneal Cross-linking (CXL) has significantly delayed the need for PKP in keratoconus patients.
Femtosecond laser-assisted keratoplasty (FLAK) provides better wound geometry (top-hat/zig-zag) compared to manual trephination.
The Collaborative Corneal Transplantation Studies (CCTS) highlight the impact of HLA matching in high-risk grafts.
